newsitem.title: USA: Christmas Season to Bring More CD-ROM Mayhem.
newsitem.headline: Christmas Season to Bring More CD-ROM Mayhem.

text.p: - Take the loudest video arcade, blow it up to the size of 10 football fields, and you've got the future -- at least the future of what's going to be on the software shelves between now and Christmas.

Welcome to E3, the largest showcase of computer games on the planet. It's a world of sensory overload, with enough visual effects to make MTV seem bland and sufficient audio power to rattle the coins in your pocket. It's the show where companies try to convince the media and retail buyers that THEIR product will be the big hit this fall.

Most companies that packed the Georgia Dome and the largest exhibit hall of the Georgia World Congress Centre tried to build a buzz for their games with full-scale demonstrations, others offered sneak peeks of games still under development, and the rest tantalized with invitation-only demonstrations of titles that, they insist, will soon be too hot to stay on the shelves.
People pushing educational games or mellower titles often found themselves unable to compete with the noise from the overwhelming abundance of explosion-filled action games.
"I blew my speakers yesterday trying to compete with the guys next door," said one product demonstrator from Hoffman + Associates as he tried to show a CD-ROM on the history of golf.

The folks at Red Orb Entertainment tried to build a quieter buzz by showing five minutes of scenes from "Riven: The Sequel to Myst." It may not be much of a challenge. Even though "Myst" debuted four years ago and spawned a host of imitators claiming to be "Myst"-like, the original game has never fallen off the best seller list. An average of 60,000 copies are bought each month.
Is Riven so much of a leap ahead that competitors will begin hawking their games as "Riven"-like?

Probably not. Although computer and software capabilities have made big leaps in four years, there were no signs from the preview that "Riven" marks any kind of quantum leap. Although there are some impressive animated sequences, players will still have to look around by dissolving from one richly-textured view to another.

"Riven's" success will depend on the intricacies of the plot, the elegance of its puzzles and the beauty of the music and artwork, something that can't be judged until the game is released this fall. For now, "Riven" simply looks like another "Myst"-like game.

For kids, Humongous Entertainment is planning a charming twist on the typical baseball simulation. "Backyard Baseball," due out in October, has 30 quirky children playing baseball in a backyard or a parking lot. One youngster insists on holding onto a Teddy bear while pitching. Another swings so hard she spins like a tornado when she misses. One drawback (at least in the demonstration version) is that the kids don't run very fast; they sort of dance to the bases.

Disney Interactive, amid all its tedious tie-ins to "Hercules" and "The Little Mermaid," may have a sleeper in "Nightmare Ned," an offbeat game about a 10-year-old whose adventures are based on the nightmare worlds of his overactive imagination.

Westwood Studios gave an invitation-only showing of some impressive video from "Blade Runner," a game based on the 1982 science fiction film that starred Harrison Ford as a cop who tracks down androids that have escaped to Earth. It's scheduled for release in early November.

For people who prefer futuristic games with some oddball humour, Simon & Schuster Interactive offered a sneak peek of "Starship Titanic." This story about a two-mile-high luxury starship that crashes into your house on its maiden voyage was written by Douglas Adams, best known for his "Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy" series.

An equally demented concept is "Shyster!" the courtroom game where players are encouraged to pack the jury, fabricate evidence, bully witnesses, accuse witnesses of using the N-word, "or just plain lie." The verdict is still out over whether Museworthy Inc. will finish it before Christmas.

Probably the most controversial game in the show was "Postal." CNN, wondering about the feelings of people who have been the victims of attacks by disgruntled postal workers, has already done a piece questioning the tastefulness of a game where the goal is to mow down screaming bystanders with Molotov cocktails, heat-seeking rockets, and flame throwers.

The game doesn't depict the main character as a postal worker. However the developers, a company aptly called Running With Scissors, has been selling the game as a "first class" shoot-'em-up featuring "chilling realism as victims actually beg for mercy, scream for their lives and pile up on the streets."
"Postal" has a unique way of quitting. If you want to leave the game, it shows you putting a gun to your head and blowing your brains out.
Although it will be marketed to adults, Andy Muir, a software engineer for "Postal," said younger teens will probably fight to get their hands on it anyway.
"We made the game we wanted to play, and everyone seems happy with it," said Muir. Because "Postal" sparked at lot of interest at the show, apparently "we made the game a LOT of people want to play."
It's hard to disagree with them. After all, if you get these guys mad, there's no telling what they'll do.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
